newsitem.title: USA: Clinton blasts fashion industry over heroin glamor.
newsitem.headline: Clinton blasts fashion industry over heroin glamor.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Wednesday accused the fashion industry of promoting heroin use by young people and said it should not try to "glamorize addiction to sell clothes."
Speaking at the White House to a U.S. Conference of Mayors forum on drug abuse, Clinton censured the fashion industry for contributing to "increasing the allure of heroin among young people."

"We now see on college campuses and in neighbourhoods heroin becoming increasingly the drug of choice," Clinton told the mayors. "And we know that part of this has to do with the images that are finding their way to our young people.

"Our society cannot say on the one hand we want to have a tough, intolerant attitude toward drugs, and on the other hand send a very different message every time there might be a little money to be made on it," Clinton said.
He was attacking the so-called "heroin chic" approach that has been used in some fashion photography, in which models pose dazed as if under the influence of drugs.
The trend has been popular in recent years in fashion magazines and various advertising campaigns by the industry, featuring gaunt models who appear to be in stupors.
Clinton praised some industry leaders for "admitting flat out that images projected in fashion photos in the last few years have made heroin addiction seem glamorous and sexy and cool."
"As some of the people in those images start to die now, it becomes obvious that that is not true," Clinton said. "You do not need to glamorize addiction to sell clothes."

White House officials said Clinton's comments were prompted, in part, by a New York Times article this week on the death of Davide Sorrenti, a 20-year-old fashion photographer whose work often captured a "heroin look."
His death in February from a drug overdose has led to soul-searching in the trendy world of fashion and the publications that cover it.
"American fashion has been an enormous source of creativity and beauty and art and, frankly, economic prosperity for the United States," Clinton said.

"But the glorification of heroin is not creative. It's destructive. It's not beautiful. It is ugly. And this is not about art. It's about life and death. And glorifying death is not good for any society," he said.
Although Clinton has been promoting his administration's anti-drug efforts, it marked the first time he has singled out the fashion industry for criticism.
The music industry and Hollywood movie makers have been the target of criticism in the past, prompting leaders in both fields to increase efforts to stop the glamorous portrayal of drug use.
Retired Gen. Barry McCaffrey, the administration's drug czar, told the gathering that anti-drug efforts must concentrate on young people in order to succeed.
"If you're going to confront the drug issue, you've got to focus on kids," he said. "You've got to prevent drug use in 68 million American children."
